scenario: AITA in relation to my GF's attempt to lose weight? | I've been dating my GF for 3 years. She's upset at her current weight. She's put on about 100lbs since we started dating. I've never mentioned it because she has bipolar disorder, and as I struggle with depression I fully understand how food can take the edge off when you get seriously overwhelmed with depression. But for health reasons and of course other reasons, of course I would like for her to get back to a healthy weight. My girlfriend's bipolar disorder has been a challenge for me, as where I would normally be assertive in a relationship on issues - I often have to back down in arguments because she responds poorly to being challenged. I often feel like I'm walking on ice, but I do my best to try understand her and work at helping her and supporting her as best I can. She is not happy with her current weight, and constantly remarks about it and has been complaining about it for over a year without doing anything about it. I tell her we can work on it together as a team, and both fix our diet. I feel this is the best way to go about it, rather than telling her that SHE needs to lose weight. I don't want her feeling like I'm initiating it, or that it's a journey she needs to take alone. Or that I'm pushing her to do it. For it to be a healthy journey, it needs to be something she is motivated to do and if I do it with her, then it doesn't feel like it's all on her. So, last week she decided to work on her diet. She was upset today because she hasn't lost any weight yet. I told her to not worry about the short term results - that it had only been a week, but to focus on months down the line to see changes. She was extremely defeatist and said she'll never lose weight. This kinda irritated me, because it had only been a week since she started. I felt like she hadn't fully committed, because she was drinking soft drinks and eating chips which are high in carbs so I brought that up, if she wants to see results quicker - that cutting out the junk food completely (rather than cutting down) will help her. Now I understand she's trying to make a change, but the defeatist attitude after only a week is difficult to work with. She then got angry at me and told me to "stop arguing with me about my weight". To which I replied that I wasn't, I had never in our entire relationship brought up her weight, and was just discussing her diet and how she was eating and drinking things that will make her progress slower. She then told me to drop it and leave it alone, and is now in a huff with me for the past few hours over it. I understand this is the nature of her bipolar disorder, and she will shut down anything she's challenged about something. Am I the asshole for challenging her defeatist attitude on her results, when she was taking short-cuts with junk food?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being an asshole in this situation with my girlfriend. Let me start by understanding the situation better. We've been dating for three years, and she's been struggling with her weight, having gained about 100 pounds since we started dating. I know she has bipolar disorder, and I struggle with depression myself, so I understand how food can be a coping mechanism when you're overwhelmed. I've never mentioned her weight directly because I don't want to hurt her or make her feel bad, especially considering her mental health challenges. However, I'm concerned about her health and would like her to get back to a healthy weight. I suggested that we work on our diet together as a team, thinking that this approach would be more supportive and less pressure on her. I wanted to make sure she didn't feel like I was initiating the change or that it was something she had to do alone. I emphasized that it should be a journey she's motivated to undertake, and doing it together would make it feel less lonely. Last week, she decided to work on her diet, but today she was upset because she hasn't lost any weight yet. I tried to reassure her that it's only been a week and that she should focus on the long-term changes rather than short-term results. But she became very defeatist, saying she'll never lose weight. This frustrated me because I felt like she hadn't fully committed to the change, especially since she was still drinking soft drinks and eating chips, which are high in carbs. I brought this up, suggesting that cutting out junk food completely could help her see quicker results. She got angry at me and told me to "stop arguing with me about my weight." I tried to explain that I wasn't bringing up her weight but was just discussing her diet and how her eating habits were affecting her progress. She told me to drop it and leave it alone, and she's been upset with me for the past few hours. Now, I'm wondering if I'm being an asshole by challenging her defeatist attitude and pointing out that she's taking shortcuts with junk food. I understand that her bipolar disorder makes her sensitive to being challenged about things, and she tends to shut down when she feels criticized. So, is it wrong of me to push her on this? Am I being too harsh or insensitive? On one hand, I want to support her and help her make positive changes for her health. On the other hand, I don't want to come across as critical or judgmental, especially considering her mental health struggles. Maybe I should have approached the conversation differently. Instead of pointing out her lack of commitment, I could have offered more encouragement and support. I could have acknowledged how difficult it is to make these changes and reaffirmed my commitment to helping her through this process together. I also need to consider her feelings and how she perceives my involvement. She might feel like I'm policing her or not respecting her autonomy, which could lead to her shutting down or becoming defensive. It's important to balance my concern for her health with respect for her feelings and boundaries. Perhaps in the future, I can find ways to support her without making her feel criticized. This might involve focusing on small, achievable goals and celebrating progress, no matter how minor. It's also crucial to communicate in a way that makes her feel supported rather than judged. In this specific instance, I might have overstepped by pushing her too hard, especially when she was already feeling defeated. It's possible that my approach came across as more critical than supportive, which could have contributed to her anger and withdrawal. So, reflecting on this, I think there's a better way to handle such situations in the future. By being more empathetic, supportive, and less focused on criticism, I can help create a more positive and encouraging environment for her to make the changes she wants without feeling pressured or judged.
